title: Chapter 6: RDS Deep Dive: Engines, Instance Types, and Storage

questions.q: Which instance classes should you choose for RDS for SQL Server, and why?
options: Graviton (g-suffix) classes like db.r7g — they are cheapest and fully support SQL Server
Intel/AMD i-family classes (e.g., db.r7i, db.m7i) — Graviton ARM classes do not support SQL Server on RDS
T-series burstable classes for sustained production OLTP
Any class; the engine runs identically on all of them
questions.explain: The chapter states Graviton-based instance classes are not available for SQL Server on RDS — choose the Intel/AMD i-family classes for SQL Server workloads.

questions.q: A 100 GB gp2 volume delivers which IOPS characteristics?
options: A flat 3000 IOPS with no bursting
300 IOPS baseline (3 IOPS/GB) with burst to 3000 IOPS using credits
16000 IOPS baseline regardless of size
The same 3000 IOPS baseline as a 100 GB gp3 volume
questions.explain: The chapter explains gp2 delivers 3 IOPS per GB with a burst pool for volumes under 1 TB — so 100 GB gets 300 IOPS baseline bursting to 3000 — while gp3 gives 3000 IOPS regardless of size.

questions.q: RDS storage autoscaling triggers and behaves how?
options: It triggers when free storage drops below 10% (or 5 GB) and only ever increases storage — it never shrinks
It shrinks storage automatically when data is deleted
It triggers at 50% free space and requires a reboot
It is enabled by default with no ceiling
questions.explain: The chapter states autoscaling triggers when free storage drops below 10% of allocated (or 5 GB), only increases storage, and you cannot reduce allocated storage without migrating.

questions.q: What storage monitoring practice does the chapter recommend?
options: Alarm at 5% free storage and rely on autoscaling
Only watch CPUUtilization; storage takes care of itself
Disable autoscaling and let the database go read-only as a signal
Set a CloudWatch alarm at 20% free storage, since autoscaling takes 5–15 minutes and the database goes read-only at 100%
questions.explain: The chapter warns RDS puts the database in read-only mode at 100% storage and autoscaling takes 5–15 minutes, so alarm at 20% free storage rather than relying on the 10% autoscaling trigger.

questions.q: Changing the instance class on a Multi-AZ RDS instance:
options: Is instantaneous with no downtime
Requires a full snapshot restore to a new instance
Is performed on the standby first, then fails over — visible downtime is typically 30–120 seconds for the failover
Is not supported; you must recreate the instance
questions.explain: The chapter explains that on Multi-AZ, AWS applies the instance class change to the standby first and then fails over, with total visible downtime typically 30–120 seconds — versus 3–10 minutes on Single-AZ.
